Title: Make Turkey Stock From the Thanksgiving Carcass
Description: Don't throw out the turkey carcass. Put the bones in a big pot with onion, carrot, celery, a bay leaf and cold water, and simmer gently for a few hours. Strain it, cool it quickly, refrigerate or freeze it in portions. Restaurant kitchens make stock from scraps every day, and it turns into soups, gravy and risotto all winter. Title: Easy Homemade Cranberry Sauce — Make It Ahead for Thanksgiving
Description: Homemade cranberry sauce is one of the easiest Thanksgiving sides. Simmer fresh cranberries with sugar and a little water or orange juice until the berries pop, about ten minutes, then let it cool; it thickens in the fridge. Add orange zest or a pinch of cinnamon if you like. Make it a day or two ahead, one less thing on the big day. Holiday cooking tips from Chef Sal Romano.

Title: Corkage Fees — Can You Bring Your Own Wine to a Restaurant?
Description: Some restaurants let you bring your own bottle of wine and charge a corkage fee to open and serve it. Call ahead to ask if it's allowed and what the fee is, since policies and local rules vary. Don't bring a bottle that's already on their wine list, and tip on the service. For a special holiday dinner, it can be a nice way to enjoy your own bottle. More restaurant secrets on Sal's page.

Title: Cook Your Tomato Paste First — The Italian Sauce Trick
Description: Before adding liquid to a sauce, soup or stew, stir the tomato paste into the hot oil with the onions and garlic and cook it for a minute or two until it darkens to a deep brick red. It loses the raw, tinny taste and adds a rich, savory depth. Keep stirring so it doesn't burn. A small step that makes a weeknight sauce taste slow-cooked. Title: Splitting the Check at a Restaurant — Ask at the Start
Description: Going out with a big group for the holidays? If you want separate checks, tell the server when you sit down, not when the bill arrives. Some restaurants limit how many ways a check can be split, or add a gratuity for larger parties, so ask about both up front. It keeps the end of the night easy for everyone. Title: Why You Should Let Lasagna Rest Before Cutting
Description: The restaurant secret to neat squares of lasagna: let it rest after it comes out of the oven, about 15 to 30 minutes, before you cut. The sauce and cheese settle and the layers hold together instead of sliding apart. It stays plenty hot. Lasagna is also a great make-ahead dish for holiday guests. Title: Order Two Appetizers Instead of an Entree — A Smart Way to Eat Out
Description: Not very hungry, or want to try more of the menu? Order two appetizers or small plates as your dinner. It often costs less than an entree, the portions are easier to finish, and you get to taste two dishes. Just ask the server to bring them together if you want them as your main course. Title: Fresh vs Dried Pasta — Which One for Which Sauce?
Description: Fresh pasta isn't automatically better than dried. Soft fresh egg pasta goes well with butter, cream and delicate sauces. Good dried pasta, made from durum wheat semolina, holds up to tomato sauces, olive oil and hearty ragù, and it's what many Italian home cooks use every day. Look for a short ingredient list and a rough texture. Easy Italian dinner tips from Chef Sal Romano.

Title: The Anchovy Trick for Deeper Tomato Sauce
Description: Many Italian cooks melt an anchovy fillet or a little anchovy paste into the warm olive oil with the garlic before adding tomatoes. It dissolves completely and adds a savory depth that people can't quite name, without tasting fishy. Try it in marinara, puttanesca or a quick pan sauce. Skip it if someone at the table avoids fish. Title: Why Restaurant Cooks Keep Their Knives Sharp
Description: Restaurant cooks keep their knives sharp because a dull blade needs more pressure and is more likely to slip off an onion or a tomato skin. Use a honing steel often to keep the edge straight, sharpen a few times a year or have it done, cut on a wood or plastic board, and hand-wash and dry your knife. Holiday prep goes faster too. Title: How Restaurant Cooks Taste Salad Dressing — On a Leaf
Description: Restaurant cooks taste salad dressing on a piece of lettuce, not on a spoon. On its own, a dressing tastes too sharp or too salty; on a leaf, you taste it the way it'll be eaten. Adjust the salt, acid and oil from there, and dress the salad just before serving so the leaves stay crisp. Easy holiday side dish tips from Chef Sal Romano.

Title: The Restaurant Trick for a Stress-Free Holiday Dinner — Plan Backwards
Description: Restaurant kitchens run on a prep list, and it works for holiday dinners too. Start with the time you sit down and work backwards: when the turkey or roast goes in, when it rests, when sides go in the oven, what can be made a day or two ahead. Write it on paper and stick it on the fridge. Make-ahead sides free up the oven. Holiday cooking tips from Chef Sal Romano.

Title: The Secret to a Flaky Pie Crust — Keep the Butter Cold
Description: For a flaky pie crust, keep everything cold: cold butter cut into small pieces, ice water, and quick hands. Little bits of butter left in the dough turn to steam in the hot oven and puff up into flaky layers. Chill the dough before rolling and again before baking. Description: When a dish comes drowned in dressing or sauce, you can't take it back off. Ask for it on the side and add as much as you want. Most kitchens are happy to do it, and your salad stays crisp, your fries stay crunchy and the leftovers reheat better. One of the easiest restaurant ordering tips. Title: Toast Nuts Before Baking and Salads — The Easy Flavor Trick
Description: Toasting nuts brings out a deep, roasted flavor. Put walnuts, pecans or pine nuts in a dry pan over medium heat and stir often for a few minutes, or spread them on a sheet pan in the oven. Take them off as soon as they smell toasty and look a shade darker, then move them to a plate so they don't keep cooking. Great for holiday baking, stuffing and salads. Tips from Chef Sal Romano.

Description: Planning a holiday party at a restaurant? Many private rooms come with a food and beverage minimum, and some add a service charge, room fee or tax on top.
